answer.reason: The AI system is a safety component of a gas boiler product covered by Regulation (EU) 2016/426 (appliances burning gaseous fuels) listed in Annex I, Section A. The product undergoes third-party conformity assessment (EU type-examination) under that harmonisation legislation. Article 6(1) therefore classifies this as high-risk, as the system's failure to maintain proper air-to-gas ratio creates direct risks of carbon monoxide production and flame instability affecting health and safety.

The AI system is a safety component of machinery (palletizing systems) covered by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (Machinery Regulation) listed in Annex I, Section A, point 21. The system is intended to prevent injury by detecting human presence and controlling robot arm speed, making it a safety-critical component that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Machinery Regulation, thus meeting Article 6(1) conditions for high-risk classification.

The on-board assistance unit is a safety component of a rail vehicle covered by Directive (EU) 2016/797 (rail interoperability), listed in Annex I Section A point 17. The system performs critical safety functions (speed control, collision avoidance, emergency braking) and has undergone third-party conformity assessment by a notified body as required by that directive. Under Article 6(1), it qualifies as high-risk. The operator is a deployer putting the system into service under its own authority and must comply with the high-risk AI system obligations from 2 August 2028 (Article 113(3)(c)(ii)).

The door controller is an AI system that is a safety component of a lift product covered by Directive 2014/33/EU (listed in Annex I, Section A). The lift undergoes third-party conformity assessment by a notified body before placing on the market, satisfying Article 6(1). The system's failure to detect obstacles could cause physical harm to passengers, making it a safety component under Article 6(1b). High-risk classification applies from 2 August 2028 per Article 113(c)(ii), before the planned 2029 installations.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: it is not a safety component of a product under Annex I (Art. 6(1)), and while it may fall under Annex III point 5 (essential services—water management), Art. 6(3) applies because the system performs a narrow procedural task (harvest forecasting and watering recommendations) without controlling critical infrastructure or replacing human decision-making on safety-critical matters. The grower retains full control and the consequences of error are economic, not safety-related. It does not trigger Art. 50 transparency duties (no direct interaction with natural persons, no synthetic content generation). Therefore it is minimal_risk.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibited practices. It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) because, although it is a safety component of a product (the thermostat) covered by Union harmonisation legislation (Directive 2014/53/EU on radio equipment in Annex I, Section B), the product is not required to undergo third-party conformity assessment for safety reasons—radio equipment certification concerns electromagnetic compatibility and spectrum, not safety (Art. 6(1)(b), Art. 6(1c)). It is not listed in Annex III. Therefore it carries only transparency obligations under Art. 50 if applicable, but the system does not interact directly with natural persons in a way triggering Art. 50(1), nor does it generate synthetic content. The system is minimal_risk.

The system performs remote biometric identification by matching faces and voices against a reference database of known persons without their knowledge or consent. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) as a remote biometric identification system. Article 6(2) classifies such systems as high-risk, and the Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of editorial decision-making by automatically identifying and cataloguing individuals in archival material.

The system performs remote biometric identification by converting caller voices into voiceprints and matching them against a database without the caller's knowledge or consent. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) (remote biometric identification systems), which lists high-risk AI systems. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making by routing calls to specialists based on biometric matching, and it performs profiling of natural persons, which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification under Article 6(3), final sentence.

The system is designed to profile natural persons by extracting biometric data (faces and tattoos) and matching them against databases to identify suspects in criminal investigations. This falls under Annex III, point 6(e), which covers AI systems for profiling of natural persons in the course of detection and investigation of criminal offences. Article 6(3) does not apply because the system performs profiling, which the regulation explicitly states shall always be considered high-risk regardless of other conditions.

The system performs remote biometric identification by converting faces into templates and matching them against an indexed database of portraits gathered from public web sources. This falls squarely within Annex III, point 1(a), which covers remote biometric identification systems. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply: the system is not performing a narrow procedural task, is not improving a prior human activity, and is not merely detecting deviations—it actively identifies individuals. The profiling rule in Article 6(3) further confirms high-risk status.

The system performs remote biometric identification at stadium entry by comparing facial images against a stadium ban list. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) as a remote biometric identification system. Although the use case (enforcing stadium bans) may be narrower than law enforcement, Article 6(3) does not exempt it because the system performs profiling of natural persons by identifying them against a database, which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification under the profiling rule in Article 6(3), final sentence.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibited practices. It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a product in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (biometric verification for identity confirmation is excluded from Annex III(1)(a)). However, it performs biometric verification of natural persons and triggers Art. 50(3) transparency obligations for deployers of biometric categorisation and emotion recognition systems, though the system here is narrower. The system falls under Art. 50 transparency requirements as it involves direct interaction with natural persons through biometric processing, placing it in the limited_risk class.

The system performs remote biometric identification by comparing a fingerprint against a stored biometric template to verify identity during police traffic stops. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) as a biometric identification system used by law enforcement. Although the comparison is limited to a single document rather than a database, the system still constitutes biometric identification for law enforcement purposes and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III:1(a).

The system performs remote biometric identification by matching residents' faces, fingerprints, or voice against registered biometric data to control access to buildings. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) (remote biometric identification systems), making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2). The exception in Annex III, point 1(a) for biometric verification systems applies only where the sole purpose is to confirm a specific person's identity; here the system also controls physical access, so the exception does not apply.

The system performs remote biometric identification of natural persons by matching captured facial images against a registered database of festival attendees. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) (remote biometric identification systems), making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2). The deployer (festival operator) is subject to the obligations of a provider under Article 16 as they are using this high-risk system under their authority.

The system is a remote biometric identification system using facial recognition to control access to restricted areas. Article 6(2) with Annex III, point 1(a) classifies remote biometric identification systems as high-risk AI systems. The system's use for access control to sensitive facilities (research labs, server room, controlled substances vault) falls squarely within this category, regardless of the narrow procedural task exception in Article 6(3) not applying here since the system makes the access decision itself rather than merely assisting human review.

The system is deployed by a law enforcement authority (Landeskriminalamt) to evaluate the reliability of evidence in criminal investigations by pre-sorting and categorizing seized digital evidence before human review. This falls under Annex III, point 6(c), which covers AI systems intended to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of investigation or prosecution of criminal offences. The system's function of marking images containing children and grouping similar content directly supports evidence assessment in criminal proceedings.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 6(e) as it is intended to be used by law enforcement authorities for profiling of natural persons in the course of detection and investigation of criminal offences by tracking and grouping individuals across video material. Although the system does not assign names, the tracking and grouping of sightings to identify the same person across footage constitutes profiling within the meaning of Art. 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of criminal investigation decision-making and does not fall within the narrow procedural task or preparatory task categories. As a provider placing the system into service with law enforcement, the company is subject to high-risk requirements under Art. 16.

The system is deployed by law enforcement to profile natural persons by comparing facial images from investigation files to detect connections between criminal cases. This falls under Annex III, point 6(e), which covers AI systems for profiling of natural persons in the course of detection and investigation of criminal offences. Article 6(3) does not apply because the system performs profiling, which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification regardless of other conditions.

Article 5(1)(g) prohibits biometric categorisation systems that categorise natural persons based on biometric data to deduce or infer their race. The system infers ethnic origin from facial and gait biometrics and sorts passengers into groups on that basis, which directly violates this prohibition. The exception for law enforcement does not apply to airport operations.

The system performs biometric categorisation by inferring gender and age bracket from facial images of natural persons in a border control context. This falls under Annex III, point 1(b), which lists AI systems intended for biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes. As a deployer of this high-risk AI system, the border guard service must comply with the requirements in Chapter III of the AI Act, which apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems.

The system infers gender from keystroke dynamics and uses this to tailor content, constituting biometric categorisation based on inferred personal characteristics. Article 6(2) with Annex III, point 1(b) classifies AI systems for biometric categorisation of natural persons according to protected attributes as high-risk. The profiling rule in Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making (personalisation of homepage and product suggestions).

The system uses AI to categorise natural persons based on biometric data (facial features) to infer age, which constitutes biometric categorisation under Annex III, point 1(b). Although the company deploys rather than provides the system, it remains a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III. The exception in Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making (whether to dispense the product) and performs profiling, which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification under Article 6(3), final sentence.

The system infers emotional states (anger) from biometric data (facial expression, posture, gait) of natural persons to support law enforcement decision-making. This falls under Annex III, point 1(c) (emotion recognition systems). As a deployer of this high-risk AI system, the police force is subject to the obligations in Article 16 and must comply by 2 December 2027 per Article 113(3)(c)(i).

The system performs emotion recognition on natural persons by analyzing facial expressions and body language from video footage. Article 6(2) in conjunction with Annex III, point 1(c) classifies AI systems intended for emotion recognition as high-risk. Although the system is used in a game development context for design improvement rather than in workplace or education settings, the prohibition in Article 5(f) applies only to emotion recognition in those specific contexts, leaving the general high-risk classification under Annex III applicable here.

The system performs biometric categorisation by inferring physical and health characteristics (drowsiness, fainting risk) from visual biometric data (eye position, head position, posture). Article 6(2) with Annex III, point 1(b) classifies AI systems intended for biometric categorisation based on inference of characteristics as high-risk. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making (suggesting where to stop) and performs profiling of natural persons, which triggers the profiling rule in Art. 6(3) final sentence.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)): it infers responses to network traffic to reveal attack methods. It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (Annex III): it does not perform biometric identification, manage critical infrastructure, support education, recruitment, essential services, law enforcement, migration control, or judicial processes. The system does not trigger Art. 50 transparency duties (it does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content). It therefore falls under minimal_risk.

The email security service is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (Annex III): it performs narrow procedural tasks (flagging suspicious emails, scanning for leaked credentials) with human review by security analysts before any action, and does not profile natural persons or influence significant decisions about them. Art. 6(3) exceptions apply. The transparency obligation in Art. 50 does not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons. Therefore, minimal_risk applies.

The AI system controls critical infrastructure (fire detection and suppression in data centers) and qualifies as high-risk under Annex III, point 2, as an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure. The company is a deployer under Art. 3(4) using the system under its authority in its data center operations.

The speech translation tool is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5) and does not fall under high-risk categories in Annex I or III, as it performs a narrow assistive function for communication without materially influencing safety-critical decisions. However, as a provider deploying an AI system that interacts directly with natural persons (drivers and passengers), the deployer must comply with Article 50(1) transparency obligations to inform users that they are interacting with an AI system.

The traffic light control system is an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of road traffic, as it autonomously controls signal phases based on predictions of traffic flow and pedestrian movement. This falls under Annex III, point 2 (critical infrastructure). The company is a provider placing the system on the market under its own name to public authorities in the Union.

The AI system is a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure (water supply), as it detects dangerous pressure surges and automatically triggers protective valve closure. This falls under Annex III, point 2. The utility is a deployer under Article 3(4), using the AI system under its authority in the water distribution network.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) because it is not a safety component of a product covered by Annex I, nor under Art. 6(2) and Annex III because it performs a narrow procedural task of monitoring and reporting (Art. 6(3)(a)) without replacing or influencing human assessment (Art. 6(3)(c)). It does not trigger Art. 50 transparency duties because it does not interact directly with natural persons. Therefore it is minimal_risk.

The AI system is intended to be used in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure (electricity supply network), making it a high-risk AI system under Annex III, point 2 of the EU AI Act. As a regional grid operator deploying this system in its control center to monitor network status and support critical operational decisions, the company is a deployer subject to the high-risk requirements applicable from 2 December 2027 (Article 113(3)(c)(i)).

The network-detection AI system is intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure (the transmission system operator's communication networks linking substations). Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 2 classify such systems as high-risk. The deployer must comply with Chapter III requirements from 2 December 2027 onwards.

The system is an AI application that analyzes photographs of electricity meter installations to provide quality control feedback to technicians. It qualifies as an AI system under Art. 3(1) and falls within the Act's scope under Art. 2(1)(b) as the company is a deployer located in the Union. The system does not engage in prohibited practices under Art. 5, nor does it constitute a high-risk system under Art. 6: it performs a narrow procedural task of quality assurance on completed work and does not materially influence decision-making, as the technician retains full discretion over corrective actions. The system therefore triggers only the transparency obligations under Art. 50(1), requiring disclosure that natural persons (technicians) are interacting with an AI system.

The system is an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure (electricity supply), falling under Annex III, point 2. Although the system does not itself control the grid and operators retain decision-making authority, Article 6(1a) and (1b) clarify that AI systems whose failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety qualify as safety components, and the derogation in Article 6(3) does not apply because the system performs profiling-equivalent risk assessment of the grid state rather than a narrow procedural task or preparatory function.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: although it relates to critical infrastructure (Annex III, point 2), it performs only a preparatory task—analyzing historical network data to identify patterns for human review and planning, without replacing or influencing human assessment of network operations (Art. 6(3), second subparagraph, point (d)). It does not trigger transparency obligations under Art. 50. Therefore it is minimal_risk.

The electricity distribution operator is a deployer of an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure (electricity supply), falling under Annex III, point 2. Although the system provides advisory forecasts rather than direct control, it is designed to support critical infrastructure management decisions. Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making for grid operations, and the operator's use case does not qualify as a narrow procedural task, preparatory task, or mere improvement of completed human activity.

The school administration system uses AI to determine access and admission of children to educational institutions by automatically assigning school places based on address, capacity, family situation and other factors. This falls under Annex III, point 3(a), which covers AI systems intended to determine access or admission to educational institutions. The system is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, as it makes binding decisions affecting educational access without the exception conditions in Article 6(3) applying (it is not a narrow procedural task, does not merely improve prior human activity, and directly influences the outcome of admission decisions).

The system is an AI system intended to determine access to educational and vocational training institutions by assigning natural persons to apprenticeship programmes based on their qualifications and test scores, falling under Annex III, point 3(a). As a deployer using the system under its authority within the Union, the public employment agency is subject to the high-risk requirements from 2 December 2027 onwards (Article 113(3)(c)(i)), which applies before the system's deployment date of 2028.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: although it relates to education, it does not fall under Annex III, point 3, because it does not determine access/admission to institutions, evaluate learning outcomes, assess educational level, or monitor student behaviour—it merely suggests programmes to individual pupils for their own consideration, with no institutional role. Article 50(1) applies: the provider must ensure pupils are informed they are interacting with an AI system unless obvious from context.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It does not engage prohibited practices (Art. 5). Although it relates to education decisions, it falls outside high-risk classification under Art. 6(3) because it performs a preparatory task to assessment (Art. 6(3), second subparagraph, point (d)): it audits completed decisions post-hoc without replacing or influencing human assessment, and does not perform profiling. The system therefore triggers only transparency obligations under Art. 50, making it limited_risk.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the EU AI Act (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited under Art. 5. It falls under Annex III, point 3(b) as an AI system intended to evaluate learning outcomes in educational institutions. Although the system does not assign grades or make final assessments of what the child has learned, it continuously evaluates and adapts the learning process based on the child's performance and behaviour, which constitutes evaluation of learning outcomes used to steer the learning process. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system performs profiling of natural persons (children with specific needs), which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification under Art. 6(3), final sentence.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a product in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (Annex III). While it touches education, it performs a narrow preparatory task—detecting errors in a completed exam paper—and does not determine access, assign students, evaluate learning outcomes, assess educational level, or monitor student behaviour; it merely assists the teacher in quality control of their own work. Art. 6(3)(d) applies: the system performs a preparatory task to an assessment. It does not profile natural persons. Therefore it falls outside high-risk classification. Art. 50 transparency duties do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content. The system is minimal_risk.

The system is an AI system intended to determine access to or admission to educational institutions at all levels by assigning learners to different programme levels based on automated scoring of placement tests. This falls under Annex III, point 3(a). As a deployer using the licensed system under its own authority, the college is subject to high-risk AI system obligations under Article 6(2) and Chapter III (applicable from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems).

The school authority uses an AI system to determine access to and assignment of children to educational institutions and special education programs based on test results, teacher assessments, and medical data. This falls under Annex III, point 3(a), which covers AI systems intended to determine access or admission to educational institutions. The system makes consequential decisions affecting the educational pathway and support level for approximately 1,500 children annually, making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2).

The system is an AI system intended to be used to assess the appropriate level of education that an individual will receive or will be able to access, within the context of educational and vocational training institutions, falling under Annex III, point 3(c). Although the provider argues the system only reflects user input and does not replace human decision-making, the system's core function is to suggest educational programmes and certificates at levels suited to the user, which constitutes assessment of appropriate educational level. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system performs profiling of natural persons (students) to tailor educational recommendations, triggering the profiling rule that mandates high-risk classification regardless of other conditions.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a regulated product) or Art. 6(2) with Annex III, since it operates on aggregated data for research and reporting purposes, not to make decisions about individual students' access, admission, or educational placement (Annex III, point 3). The Art. 6(3) exception applies: the system performs a preparatory task to assessment (aggregating data for analysis) and does not materially influence individual decision-making. No transparency obligations under Art. 50 are triggered. The system is therefore minimal_risk.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a product in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) read with Annex III, point 3 (education), because it performs a narrow procedural task—preparing questions for a human-conducted assessment—and does not materially influence the outcome of the admission decision, which remains entirely with the human instructor (Art. 6(3)(a), (b)). The system therefore triggers transparency obligations under Art. 50(1): it must inform natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system during the assessment preparation phase.

The system is an AI tool used to evaluate learning outcomes and steer the learning process of apprentices by suggesting improvements to tutor recommendations for advanced course placement. This falls under Annex III, point 3(b), which covers AI systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes in educational institutions. Although the tool is advisory and tutors retain decision-making authority, it materially influences the outcome of decisions affecting apprentices' educational pathways, and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception as it is not merely a narrow procedural task or preparatory assessment.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the EU AI Act (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited under Art. 5. It falls under Annex III, point 3(d), as it is intended to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests in educational and vocational training institutions. The system does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) exception because it performs profiling of natural persons (monitoring individual behaviour patterns) and is not merely a narrow procedural task, improvement of prior human activity, or preparatory task.

The system monitors student behavior during online exams to detect cheating patterns using machine learning. This falls under Annex III, point 3(d) as an AI system for monitoring and detecting prohibited behavior of students during tests in educational institutions. The deployer (the university) is subject to high-risk AI system obligations under Article 6(2) and Chapter III, which applies to such systems from 2 December 2027 onwards.

The system is an AI system within the scope of Article 3(1) and Article 2. It is intended to be used for monitoring and detecting prohibited behaviour of students during tests in educational institutions, which falls under Annex III, point 3(d). Although the system supports human decision-making by the proctor rather than making autonomous decisions, Article 6(3) does not apply because the system performs profiling of natural persons (students) to detect cheating patterns, and Article 6(3) explicitly states that profiling triggers high-risk classification regardless of other conditions.

The system is an AI system intended to be used for recruitment and selection of natural persons, specifically to analyse and filter job applications and evaluate candidates by assigning scores and rankings based on CV data, test results, and comparison with job descriptions and historical hiring patterns. This falls squarely under Annex III, point 4(a), which lists AI systems intended for recruitment or selection as high-risk. The company is the provider as it develops and places the system on the market under its own name.

The sourcing tool is an AI system intended to be used for recruitment and selection of natural persons by filtering job candidates and generating shortlists based on specified criteria. This falls squarely within Annex III, point 4(a), which covers AI systems intended for recruitment or selection, including analysing and filtering job applications and evaluating candidates. As a deployer placing the system into service in the Union from 2028, the company is subject to high-risk AI system obligations under Article 6(2) and Chapter III.

The system is an AI system intended to be used for recruitment and selection of natural persons, specifically to analyse and filter job applications and evaluate candidates, which falls under Annex III, point 4(a). The company is a provider placing the system on the market under its own name. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply as the system materially influences the outcome of hiring decisions rather than performing a narrow procedural task or merely improving prior human activity.

The system is used to filter and rank job applicants for apprenticeship positions based on qualifications and personal characteristics, which falls under Annex III, point 4(a) (AI systems for recruitment and selection of natural persons). The deployer is a company established in the Union using the system under its authority to make decisions affecting access to vocational training, triggering high-risk classification under Article 6(2) and Article 3(4).

The system is an AI model that filters and targets job advertisements to members based on inferred characteristics and behavioral patterns, which constitutes recruitment or selection of natural persons. This falls under Annex III, point 4(a), which covers AI systems intended to be used for recruitment or selection, including analyzing and filtering job applications and evaluating candidates. The system materially influences the outcome of recruitment decisions by determining which candidates see which job opportunities.

The staffing agency deploys an AI system intended to be used for recruitment and selection of natural persons by ranking candidates for job vacancies and suggesting suitable vacancies to jobseekers. This falls under Annex III, point 4(a), which covers AI systems for recruitment or selection, including analysing and filtering job applications and evaluating candidates. The agency's consultants mostly follow the tool's rankings when deciding whom to put forward, making this a high-risk system under Article 6(2).

The system is intended to be used for recruitment by analyzing job advertisements to filter language before publication. Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 4(a) classify as high-risk AI systems intended to be used for recruitment or selection of natural persons, including to analyze and filter job content. Although the system does not directly evaluate candidates, it is designed to influence the recruitment process by pre-screening advertisement text, which falls within the scope of recruitment-related AI systems.

The system is an AI-based ad placement optimizer for employer-branding campaigns. It does not fall under Article 5 (prohibited practices), Article 6(1) (safety components in harmonised products), or Article 6(2) with Annex III (high-risk categories). The system performs a narrow procedural task of optimizing ad placement based on aggregate metrics and demographics, without making individual employment decisions or profiling natural persons for recruitment purposes. It therefore triggers only the transparency obligation under Article 50(1) for AI systems interacting with natural persons, classifying it as limited_risk under the Act's framework; however, since the description does not indicate direct interaction with individuals in a way that requires disclosure, and the system does not generate synthetic content, the minimal_risk classification applies.

The system is an AI tool for analyzing employer reputation trends from public sources with names removed at collection, used only for market insights into employer branding perception. It does not involve recruitment, selection, employment decisions, or individual assessment of natural persons, and therefore falls outside the high-risk categories in Annex III (employment, workers' management) and Article 6. The transparency obligations of Article 50 do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content. The system is subject only to minimal-risk obligations.

This AI system is designed to assist jobseekers in improving their own CV presentations by providing suggestions for skill emphasis and content reorganization. While it relates to recruitment, it falls under Article 50's transparency obligations rather than the high-risk categories in Annex III. The system does not make or influence employment decisions, does not evaluate candidates for employers, and does not perform profiling—it merely provides suggestions to individual users who retain full control over their CV content. Article 50(1) requires disclosure that users are interacting with an AI system, which applies here.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It does not fall under high-risk classification: although it touches employment (Annex III, point 4(a)), it performs a narrow procedural task of verification against official registers and does not score, rank, filter or influence recruitment decisions, satisfying Art. 6(3) exception conditions (a) and (b). It does not trigger transparency obligations under Art. 50. Therefore it is minimal_risk.

The system extracts and organizes information from CVs without evaluating, scoring, filtering or ranking candidates. It performs a narrow procedural task of data extraction and structuring, which falls outside the high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, point 4(a) (recruitment AI systems that analyse and filter applications or evaluate candidates). Article 50 transparency obligations do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons. The system therefore qualifies as minimal_risk.

The scheduling system is an AI system intended to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, allocation of tasks based on individual behaviour and personal traits, and monitoring and evaluation of worker performance and behaviour. This falls squarely under Annex III, point 4(b). The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it performs profiling of natural persons (workers) and materially influences the outcome of employment decisions, making it high-risk.

The AI system provides personalized learning recommendations and feedback to employees based on quiz results and course progress on a voluntary learning platform. This falls under Article 50(1) transparency obligations, as the system interacts directly with natural persons (employees) and they must be informed they are interacting with an AI system. The system does not qualify as high-risk under Annex III because it performs a preparatory task to assessment (Article 6(3)(d)) and does not materially influence employment decisions, as the feedback is not used for recruitment, performance evaluation, promotion, or termination decisions.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It does not engage prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: it does not fall under Art. 6(1) (no product safety component in Annex I), nor under Art. 6(2) and Annex III (not biometric identification, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or justice). Art. 6(3) does not apply as the system is not listed in Annex III. The system does not trigger Art. 50 transparency duties (it does not interact directly with natural persons in a way that requires disclosure, nor generate synthetic content). It therefore falls under minimal_risk.

The system is an AI-based writing assistant that improves language and style in promotion reports after human decision-making is complete, without altering substantive content or decisions. It does not fall under Article 5 prohibitions, Article 6 high-risk categories (it is not a safety component, nor does it fall under Annex III as it performs a narrow preparatory task of text refinement with human review), and while it may trigger Article 50 transparency obligations for AI systems interacting with natural persons, the primary classification is minimal_risk as a deployer using an AI system for post-decision text processing.

The system evaluates eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits (unemployment benefits) and proposes grant or denial decisions, falling under Annex III, point 5(a). The deployer is a public authority using the AI system under its authority to make or support decisions on benefit eligibility, making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and (3). The telephone system is out of scope as it is not an AI system within Article 3(1).

The municipality is deploying an AI system to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits (social housing and supplementary unemployment allowance) as described in Annex III, point 5(a). The system makes risk assessments that materially influence caseworker decisions on benefit allocation, falling squarely within high-risk classification under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 5(a), which covers AI systems used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public services and benefits.

The system is a deployer of an AI system that evaluates eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits (healthcare and social services) and makes decisions on granting or reducing such benefits under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 5(a). The allocation of limited care hours to vulnerable elderly persons based on automated assessment of needs, care level, and waiting times constitutes a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act, as it directly affects access to essential public services for a vulnerable population.

The system evaluates eligibility for essential public assistance benefits (sickness pay) and determines whether to grant, reduce, or withhold such benefits by flagging claims for investigation and holding payment. This falls under Annex III, point 5(a), which covers AI systems used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and to grant, reduce, revoke, or reclaim such benefits. The deployer is a public authority (national sickness-insurance agency) using the system under its authority to make decisions affecting benefit entitlements.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1)) that evaluates eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, specifically healthcare services, and determines access to them by deciding whom to invite to screening programmes. This falls squarely under Annex III, point 5(a), which covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services. The deployer is a public authority (regional health agency) using the system under its authority (Art. 3(4)), making it a deployer subject to high-risk obligations from 2 December 2027 (Art. 113(3)(c)(i))

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 5(a), as it is intended to be used by a public authority to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services and to grant or allocate such benefits by routing applications to the appropriate team for decision-making. Although the system itself does not make the final eligibility determination, it materially influences the outcome by determining which team handles the application, and thus qualifies as high-risk under Art. 6(2) without meeting the Art. 6(3) exceptions (it is not a narrow procedural task, does not improve a completed activity, and is not merely preparatory).

The system evaluates eligibility for and determines amounts of essential public benefits (subsidies/grants) provided by a public authority. This falls under Annex III, point 5(a), which covers AI systems intended to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services and to grant or reduce such benefits. Although human review occurs at the final payment stage, the system's core function is to assess and propose reimbursement decisions on subsidy applications, making it high-risk under Article 6(2) and (3).

The system is an AI system intended to be used by a public authority (the health-insurance fund) to evaluate eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits (healthcare benefits such as home nursing and medical devices). Although the system performs a preparatory task by retrieving and presenting facts rather than making the eligibility decision itself, Article 6(3) does not exempt it because it materially influences the outcome of decision-making by the caseworkers who rely on its factual outputs to assess eligibility. The system falls under Annex III, point 5(a), and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) derogation.

The system is an AI translation service used by a public authority to assist caseworkers in processing social assistance applications. It does not make or influence decisions on eligibility for benefits; the caseworker retains full decision-making authority after reviewing both the translation and original. Article 6(3) exceptions apply: the system performs a preparatory task (translation) to an assessment relevant for Annex III, point 5(a), and does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making. The transparency obligations of Article 50 do not apply as the system does not interact directly with applicants. The system therefore falls outside high-risk classification and is subject only to minimal-risk obligations.

The bank is deploying an AI system intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons and establish their credit score for the purpose of making loan decisions affecting access to essential private services (credit). This falls under Annex III, point 5(b), which lists AI systems for creditworthiness evaluation as high-risk. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making on loan approvals and is not merely a narrow procedural task or preparatory assessment.

The company develops and places on the market an AI system that evaluates the creditworthiness of natural persons and establishes their credit score. This falls under Annex III, point 5(b), which lists AI systems intended to evaluate creditworthiness or establish credit scores as high-risk. The system is placed on the market when it goes into operation in 2028, and the company is the provider under Article 3(3) as it develops the system and places it into service under its own name.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibitions. It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a regulated product) or Art. 6(2) with Annex III, because although it relates to creditworthiness assessment (Annex III, 5(b)), it performs only a preparatory task—plain-language explanation and real-time feedback on form completion—and does not itself evaluate creditworthiness or establish credit scores; the actual credit assessment is performed separately by underwriters. Art. 6(3) applies: the system does not pose significant risk because it is preparatory and does not materially influence the outcome of the credit decision. However, the system is intended to interact directly with natural persons (applicants), triggering Art. 50(1) transparency obligations: users must be informed they are interacting with an AI system.

The AI system evaluates creditworthiness of natural persons to determine eligibility for margin lending, which falls under Annex III, point 5(b) (AI systems intended to evaluate creditworthiness or establish credit scores). Although the system is limited to margin lending rather than consumer credit, it still assesses credit risk for the purpose of granting financial services. The portfolio-analysis screen does not change this classification as it serves a different function.

The analytics platform is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(b)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) because it is not a safety component of a product covered by Annex I. Under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, point 5(c), it could fall within life and health insurance risk assessment, but Art. 6(3) applies: the system performs a preparatory task to assessment (designing policies before individual underwriting occurs) and does not assess or influence decisions on individual customers. The financial-literacy programme is not an AI system. The system therefore carries only transparency obligations under Art. 50, which do not apply here as it does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content.

The system evaluates and classifies emergency calls by natural persons and establishes priority in dispatching emergency first response services (police, firefighters, medical aid), falling squarely under Annex III, point 5(d). Although the system makes dispatch decisions automatically, the deployer (the integrated emergency control center) remains responsible as the entity using the AI system under its authority to perform these high-risk functions affecting emergency response outcomes.

The system is intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons and to establish priority in dispatching emergency first response services (ambulance), falling under Annex III, point 5(d). The deployer is the ambulance service using the system under its authority to assist in emergency call triage and dispatch prioritization, which materially influences the outcome of emergency response decisions.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 5(d) as an AI system intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls and establish priority in dispatching emergency first response services. The deployer (nursing home operator) is subject to high-risk obligations under Art. 6(2) and Chapter III from 2 December 2027 (Art. 113(3)(c)(i)).

The system is an AI system within the scope of Article 3(1) and Article 2. It evaluates and classifies emergency calls and assists in dispatching emergency first response services (fire brigades) by providing recommendations on resource allocation, falling under Annex III, point 5(d). Although human decision-makers retain final authority, the system's core function of evaluating emergency situations and recommending dispatch priorities constitutes a high-risk use case under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment) or Art. 6(2) with Annex III: while it touches on critical infrastructure and emergency response, it performs only preparatory and analytical tasks (flood mapping, wildfire spread modelling, social media monitoring) without making decisions about emergency dispatch or resource allocation, and thus falls within Art. 6(3)(d) (preparatory task to assessment). The transparency obligation in Art. 50(1) applies because the system interacts directly with natural persons (regional governments, insurers, and the public via the free heat-wave map), requiring disclosure that they are interacting with an AI system unless obvious from context.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 2 as an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical infrastructure (civil-protection agencies managing emergencies). The derogation in Art. 6(3) does not apply: the system materially influences decision-making by trainers and responders through realistic incident simulation and performance feedback, and it performs profiling of natural persons (measuring response times and identifying missed playbook steps of individual team members), which triggers the profiling rule in Art. 6(3) that overrides all derogation conditions.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: although it monitors emergency calls, it performs a narrow procedural task (real-time traffic visualization and fault detection) without making decisions affecting emergency dispatch, triage, or resource allocation, and does not materially influence the outcome of decision-making by emergency services (Art. 6(3), Annex III point 5(d) exception). It triggers transparency obligations under Art. 50(1) because it interacts with or processes data related to emergency call handling, requiring disclosure to relevant stakeholders that AI is in use.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1)) used by a public authority deployer in the Union (Art. 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5) or high-risk categories: it performs a narrow procedural task of bed and room scheduling based on medical data, does not make decisions affecting treatment or discharge (physicians retain that authority), and does not profile natural persons or materially influence outcomes of clinical decision-making (Art. 6(3)). However, it processes personal data of patients and generates predictions about individuals, triggering the transparency obligation under Art. 50(1) to inform patients that they are interacting with or subject to an AI system, unless obvious from context.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 5(d) as an AI system intended to evaluate and classify emergency situations and establish priority in dispatching emergency first response services. Although human review occurs before any action, the system performs profiling-adjacent risk assessment of geographic areas and resource allocation that materially influences the outcome of emergency response decisions, and does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) exceptions (it is not merely a narrow procedural task, preparatory task, or improvement of prior activity, and it performs more than detection of deviations). As a deployer placing the system into service from 2028, you are subject to high-risk requirements under Art. 16 by 2 December 2027 per Art. 113(3)(i).

The system is an AI system intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls and assist in dispatching emergency first response services by identifying injured persons and their locations at incident scenes. This falls under Annex III, point 5(d), which covers AI systems for emergency triage and dispatch prioritization. The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it performs profiling of natural persons (identifying and locating injured individuals) and materially influences emergency response decisions.

The system assesses the risk of a natural person becoming a victim of criminal offences (intimate partner violence) and is intended to be used by a judicial authority to assist in decision-making on protective measures. This falls under Annex III, point 6(d), which covers AI systems for assessing risk of victimization in law enforcement and judicial contexts. The system is deployed by a public authority (Austrian criminal justice) and materially influences judicial decisions on restraining orders.

The system is an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences (trafficking), falling under Annex III, point 6(a). The police force is a deployer using the system under its authority. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply: the system performs profiling of natural persons and materially influences the outcome of decision-making (triggering protection interviews), so it remains high-risk despite being a narrow procedural task.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 2, as an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of road traffic. Although it does not profile natural persons and performs a narrow procedural task of identifying high-risk locations and times, it materially influences the outcome of decision-making on patrol placement and speed-check deployment, and thus qualifies as high-risk under Art. 6(2) and (3).

The police department is deploying an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to manage critical infrastructure (crowd safety at large public events). This falls under Annex III, point 2 (critical infrastructure - road traffic and public safety management). The system qualifies as high-risk under Article 6(2) because it is designed to assess and predict safety risks in publicly accessible spaces during large-scale events, which is a core law enforcement safety function that materially influences operational decisions.

The system is used by a public authority to evaluate eligibility for essential public services (emergency response and civil protection) and to determine which natural persons receive emergency assistance, falling under Annex III, point 5(a). The flood and wildfire models assess exposure of villages and care homes to inform evacuation planning and emergency warnings, which constitutes a high-risk use case under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 5(a), as it directly influences the allocation of emergency resources and protection of vulnerable populations.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 6(c) as an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement to evaluate the reliability of evidence in criminal investigations. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system performs profiling of natural persons (assessing credibility based on facial movements and eye responses), which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification per Art. 6(3), final sentence.

The wearable system is designed to monitor occupational health and safety during police operations by detecting fatigue and physical overload, providing alerts to the wearer and medical personnel. It does not perform profiling, decision-making about personnel, or any of the high-risk functions listed in Annex III (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment decisions, essential services, law enforcement risk assessment, migration, or justice). Article 50 transparency obligations do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons in the prohibited manner. The system falls outside high-risk classification under Article 6(3) as it performs a narrow occupational safety task without influencing personnel decisions.

The system is an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of investigation or prosecution of criminal offences, falling under Annex III, point 6(c). The company is a provider placing the system on the market under its own name. Article 6(2) and (3) apply; the system does not qualify for the derogation in Article 6(3) because it materially influences the outcome of criminal investigations and does not merely perform a narrow procedural task or preparatory function.

The system is deployed by a law enforcement authority (Landeskriminalamt) to evaluate the reliability of evidence in criminal investigations, which falls under Annex III, point 6(c). The system assesses witness statements and informant tips by checking internal consistency, alignment with facts, and source reliability history—all core functions of evidence evaluation. Article 6(2) and (3) apply; the system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions because it materially influences investigative decision-making and does not merely perform a narrow procedural task or preparatory function.

The system is deployed by a law enforcement authority (national police) to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of investigation of criminal offences, falling under Annex III, point 6(c). Although the tool is a technical aid for data recovery rather than autonomous decision-making, it materially influences what evidence becomes available to investigators and thus the outcome of criminal investigations, and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions since it is not a narrow procedural task, does not improve a previously completed human activity, and is not merely preparatory.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the EU AI Act (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is intended to be used by judicial authorities and law enforcement to assist in researching and interpreting facts in the administration of justice, falling under Annex III, point 8(a). The system does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) exception because it materially influences the outcome of decision-making by investigators through its 3D reconstruction and analysis of crime scenes, rather than performing only a narrow procedural task or preparatory function.

The system is deployed by a law enforcement authority (Landeskriminalamt) to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the investigation of criminal offences (child sexual abuse material), which falls under Annex III, point 6(c). Although the system performs a preparatory task by pre-sorting material rather than making final determinations, it still qualifies as high-risk because it materially influences the outcome of investigative decision-making by prioritizing which evidence investigators examine first.

The system is an AI tool used by a judicial authority (public prosecutor's office) to assist in researching and interpreting facts and evidence in criminal cases by indexing and tagging financial documents. This falls squarely within Annex III, point 8(a), which covers AI systems intended to assist judicial authorities in researching and interpreting facts and the law. The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions because it performs more than a narrow procedural task or preparatory function—it actively processes and categorizes evidence to influence investigative decisions, and the deployer's human review does not eliminate the high-risk classification when the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making in criminal proceedings.

The system assesses the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending based on profiling, past criminal behaviour, and personal characteristics, falling under Annex III, point 6(d). As a public authority deploying this AI system for law enforcement purposes (criminal justice administration), the deployer must comply with high-risk AI system requirements under Article 6(2) and Chapter III, which apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems.

The system assesses the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending and is intended to be used by law enforcement authorities and judicial authorities in the course of criminal prosecution and sentencing. Article 6(2) read with Annex III, point 6(d) classifies such AI systems as high-risk. The system does not fall within Article 6(3)'s exceptions because it directly influences judicial decision-making on sentences and conditions rather than performing a narrow procedural task or merely improving prior human assessment.

This is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not engage prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: it predicts risk for places and times only, not for natural persons, and thus falls outside Annex III (which covers profiling and assessment of persons). It triggers transparency obligations under Art. 50(1) only if it interacts directly with natural persons, which patrol planning does not. The system is therefore subject only to minimal-risk obligations.

The system assesses the risk of natural persons offending or re-offending by analyzing sex-offender profiles, past criminal behavior, and behavioral patterns to rank suspects in criminal investigations. This falls under Annex III, point 6(d), which covers AI systems intended to assess the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending not solely on the basis of profiling. The system is placed on the market by a provider (the company) to deployers (police forces) and is therefore subject to high-risk AI system requirements under Article 6(2).

The system is an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to assess the risk of criminal offences occurring in specific areas, which falls under Annex III, point 6(a). The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it materially influences the outcome of decision-making regarding police deployment and prevention measures, and does not merely perform a narrow procedural task or preparatory function.

The system is an AI model used by law enforcement (the financial intelligence unit of the police) to assess the risk of natural persons offending or re-offending in the context of criminal investigation, specifically money laundering and terrorist financing. This falls under Annex III, point 6(d), which covers AI systems intended to assess the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending. The deployer is the financial intelligence unit, which is part of law enforcement, and the system is placed into service on 2028-10-10, after the application date of Chapter III Section 1 (2 December 2027 for Annex III systems).

The described AI systems perform narrow procedural back-office tasks (invoice processing, asset tracking, roster drafting) that do not involve decision-making about individuals' rights, performance evaluation, or law enforcement investigations. Article 6(3) excludes from high-risk classification AI systems intended to perform narrow procedural tasks, improve prior human activity, or perform preparatory tasks. None of the systems described fall within Annex III high-risk categories, and they do not trigger Article 5 prohibitions or Article 50 transparency duties.

The system is an AI system assessing risk of criminal offences by matching vehicle plates against investigation lists, deployed by a law enforcement authority. It falls under Annex III, point 6(d), which covers AI systems assessing the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending. Although the system reads plates rather than faces, it is used to identify vehicles linked to persons suspected of criminal activity, thereby assessing risk associated with natural persons. Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of law enforcement decision-making (alerting officers to investigate). The system is subject to high-risk requirements under Chapter III from 2 December 2027.

The system is an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement authorities (police and customs) to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of investigation or prosecution of criminal offences by detecting weapons, suspicious packages, dangerous substances, and stolen cultural goods from wanted lists. This falls under Annex III, point 6(c), making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2). The company is the provider placing the system on the market under its own name.

The system is a law enforcement AI intended to assess the risk of natural persons becoming victims of criminal offences by detecting suspicious movements and behaviours in railway stations, falling under Annex III, point 6(a). The deployer is a law enforcement authority using the system under its authority to support law enforcement operations, and the system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it performs ongoing monitoring and risk assessment rather than a narrow procedural task, preparatory task, or improvement of prior human activity.

The gunshot detection system is an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to assess the risk of a natural person becoming the victim of criminal offences (gunshot incidents), falling under Annex III, point 6(a). The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) derogation because it performs a core law enforcement function rather than a narrow procedural task, preparatory task, or post-hoc improvement, and it materially influences law enforcement decision-making by triggering immediate alerts to police.

The asylum office is a deployer using an AI system for migration and asylum management. The speech-to-text and translation tool is intended to be used by a competent public authority in the context of asylum processing to assist in examining applications for asylum and assessing eligibility, which falls under Annex III, point 7(d) (detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons in migration, asylum or border control management). Although the tool performs a narrow procedural task (transcription and translation) and caseworkers review outputs, it still materially influences the outcome of asylum decisions by creating the written record on which eligibility assessments depend, making it high-risk under Article 6(2) and (3).

This is a summarization tool for administrative record-keeping that does not assess credibility, make recommendations, or influence decision-making outcomes. It performs a narrow procedural task of documenting hearing content in sequence without weighting or evaluation, with human review and correction built in. Article 50 transparency obligations apply, but no high-risk classification under Article 6 is triggered.

The system is designed to assist migration and asylum authorities in processing applicants by detecting and identifying natural persons through facial landmark marking, which falls under Annex III, point 7(d) (AI systems for detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons in migration, asylum or border control management). The system qualifies as high-risk under Article 6(2) read with Annex III, as it materially influences the outcome of asylum proceedings by enabling caseworkers to better identify and assess applicants based on enhanced facial features.

The system assesses risk posed by natural persons entering the territory, making it an AI system for migration and border control management under Annex III, point 7(b). As a public authority deploying this system without modification, the border guard is a deployer subject to high-risk requirements under Article 6(2) and Chapter III (applicable from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems per Article 113(3)(c)(i)).

The system is an AI system within the scope of the EU AI Act (Art. 3(1)) used by a public authority (visa section of an EU Member State's foreign ministry) to assess risks posed by natural persons applying for visas, including security risk, irregular migration risk, and health risk. This falls squarely under Annex III, point 7(b), which lists as high-risk 'AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assess a risk, including a security risk, a risk of irregular migration, or a health risk, posed by a natural person who intends to enter or who has entered into the territory of a Member State.' The deployer is the public authority operating the system; the service provider is a third party. The system does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) exception because it performs profiling and influences the outcome of visa decisions, not merely a narrow procedural task or preparatory assessment.

The system assesses risk of irregular migration posed by natural persons entering Member State territory based on vehicle journey timing patterns, which falls squarely within Annex III, point 7(b) (AI systems assessing risk of irregular migration). Article 6(2) classifies such systems as high-risk. The company is the provider under Article 3(3), having developed and placed the system into service under its own name with a border authority from 2028.

The system is intended to assess risk of irregular migration posed by natural persons entering Member State territory, which falls under Annex III, point 7(b). Although the system performs a narrow procedural task and improves human decision-making, it performs profiling of natural persons based on group-level patterns applied to individuals, which under Article 6(3) makes it always high-risk regardless of the derogation conditions.

The system processes only aggregated data that cannot identify individuals and produces trend analysis and forecasting for policy planning. It does not fall under Annex III Article 6(2) high-risk categories for migration management (Article 6(2) and Annex III:7 require systems assessing risks posed by individual natural persons or detecting/identifying them), nor does it engage in prohibited practices under Article 5. The transparency obligations of Article 50 do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not engage any prohibited practice (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: although it processes records from immigration assessments, it performs only post-decision data tidying and deduplication, plays no role in risk assessment or decision-making, and qualifies for the Art. 6(3) exception as a preparatory task that does not materially influence outcomes. It does not trigger Art. 50 transparency duties. It is therefore minimal_risk.

The asylum authority is a deployer of an AI system intended to assist in examining asylum applications and assessing the reliability of evidence, which falls under Annex III, point 7(c). The system evaluates document authenticity, consistency of statements, and credibility—core factors in asylum eligibility assessment. Article 6(2) and (3) apply; the system does not qualify for the derogation since it materially influences the outcome of asylum decisions and performs profiling of natural persons through credibility assessment.

The system is deployed by a public authority to assist in examining asylum applications and assessing the reliability of evidence in migration proceedings, which falls under Annex III, point 7(c). The system materially influences the outcome of decision-making on asylum eligibility by providing signals that caseworkers rely upon when determining protection status, and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions as it performs more than a narrow procedural task or mere improvement of prior human activity.

The system is an AI system intended to assist competent public authorities in examining applications for asylum, visa or residence permits by detecting document manipulation and verifying authenticity, which falls under Annex III, point 7(c). The system is placed on the market by the provider under its own name and trademark for use by migration and asylum authorities, making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1)) used by a public authority for migration and asylum management. It is intended to assist in detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons by analysing linguistic features to infer country or region of origin, which falls under Annex III, point 7(d). The deployer is a public authority using the system under its authority (Art. 3(4)), making it a deployer subject to high-risk obligations from 2 December 2027 (Art. 113(3)(c)(i))—before the stated deployment date of 2028.

The system performs a narrow procedural task of document sorting into preset categories without ranking, filtering, or influencing decision-making outcomes. Article 6(3) exempts AI systems from high-risk classification where they perform narrow procedural tasks or improve results of previously completed human activity, and this system qualifies as it merely organizes documents for human review without materially influencing the outcome of immigration decisions. Article 50 transparency obligations do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content.

The system performs technical validation of visa applications (checking mandatory fields, formats, and document uploads) and distributes completed files to staff based on objective criteria like visa type and application date. This is a narrow procedural task that does not materially influence decision-making outcomes, falling within Article 6(3) exception (b) as it improves the result of previously completed human activity. However, Article 50(1) applies: the system interacts with natural persons submitting visa applications, so they must be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless this is obvious from context.

The system reads passport data to assess visa eligibility and processes applications for asylum, visa or residence permits under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 7(c). Although the system applies only fixed rules without discretion, it is intended to assist in examining visa applications and determining eligibility, which falls within the high-risk category. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of visa processing decisions by routing applicants based on nationality and passport type.

The system performs a narrow procedural task of validating technical completeness of visa application files without assessing risk, prioritizing applicants, or influencing substantive decision-making. Article 6(3) exempts AI systems in Annex III that perform narrow procedural tasks and do not materially influence outcomes. Although visa processing falls within Annex III(7)(c), this system's purely technical validation function does not pose significant risk to fundamental rights and qualifies for the exemption.

The system is deployed by a public authority (asylum office) to assist in researching and interpreting facts and law in the administration of justice by analyzing decision-making patterns in completed asylum procedures. This falls under Annex III, point 8(a), which covers AI systems assisting judicial authorities in applying law to concrete facts. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply because the system performs profiling of natural persons (asylum applicants) by analyzing their characteristics across similar constellations, which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification under Article 6(3), final sentence.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 7(d) as an AI system intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities in the context of border control management for the purpose of detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons. The company is the provider placing the system on the market under its own brand (Art. 3(3)). Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of border interception decisions and does not fall within the narrow procedural task or preparatory task exceptions.

The maritime surveillance system is used by a coast guard (public authority) for law enforcement and border control in the context of migration, asylum and border control management. Article 2(3) of the AI Act explicitly excludes AI systems placed on the market or put into service exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the entity type. Maritime border surveillance and interception operations fall within national security and defence competences, placing this system outside the Act's scope.
