The AI system is intended to detect and identify natural persons in the context of maritime operations, which falls under Annex III, point 7(d) (migration, asylum and border control management). Although the deployer's stated purpose is life-saving rather than border control, the system's capability to detect and recognize natural persons in migration contexts makes it high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III. The exception in Article 6(3) does not apply because the system performs identification of natural persons and materially influences the outcome of emergency response decisions.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibitions. It qualifies as high-risk under Art. 6(2) and Annex III, point 7(d), as it is intended to be used by border control authorities in the context of migration, asylum or border control management for the purpose of detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons. Although the system itself performs only image enhancement and does not directly detect or identify, it is designed and deployed as an integral part of the border guards' identification workflow, materially influencing the outcome of their assessment. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system is not performing a narrow procedural task, preparatory task, or improving a previously completed assessment in isolation; it is a core component of the identification process.

The system is an AI system intended to assist judicial authorities in applying the law to concrete facts by generating draft judgments and payment orders, which falls under Annex III, point 8(a). Although the system performs a preparatory task (generating a draft for human review and signature), it materially influences the outcome of decision-making in judicial proceedings, and the profiling rule does not apply here, so the Art. 6(3) exception does not eliminate the high-risk classification.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the Act (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 8(a), as it is intended to assist a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and law and in applying the law to a concrete set of facts. Although the system performs a preparatory task and the judge retains final decision-making authority, Art. 6(3) does not exempt it because it materially influences the outcome of decision-making through its proposed outcomes and judgment text, and does not fall within the narrow procedural task or preparatory task exceptions when the system's output directly shapes judicial reasoning and conclusions.

The AI system is intended to assist judicial authorities in researching and interpreting facts and law and applying law to concrete facts, falling squarely under Annex III, point 8(a). Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making by analysing facts and identifying applicable law, rather than performing a narrow procedural task, improving a prior human activity, or serving as preparatory work. The courts administration is a deployer under Article 3(4) using the system under its authority.

The case scheduling tool is an AI system intended to be used by a judicial authority (the court) to assist in administering justice by distributing cases among judges. Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 8(a) classify as high-risk AI systems those intended to assist judicial authorities in applying law to concrete facts or in a similar administrative function. Although the tool performs only case assignment based on judge specialisation and availability rather than substantive legal analysis, it materially influences the outcome of judicial proceedings by determining which judge handles each case, and thus falls within the scope of Annex III:8:a.

The system is an AI tool used by a judicial authority (Landgericht Hessen) to assist in organizing and searching evidence materials in criminal proceedings. It performs preparatory and organizational tasks—extracting events, creating chronologies, and enabling searches—without influencing judicial decision-making, which remains entirely with the judges. This falls under Article 50's transparency obligations for AI systems interacting with or assisting judicial processes, rather than Article 6(2) Annex III point 8(a), as it does not assist in researching, interpreting facts, or applying law to concrete facts.

The system is deployed by a judicial authority (Spanish appeals court) to assist in the administration of justice by processing and preparing case materials before judgment publication and by supporting case intake procedures. Article 6(2) with Annex III, point 8(a) classifies AI systems intended to assist judicial authorities in researching, interpreting facts and law, or applying law to concrete facts as high-risk. The system's role in preparing judicial documents and supporting case administration falls within this scope, even though it does not directly influence judicial decision-making.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the EU AI Act (Art. 3(1)), as it infers and extracts structured data (party identities and addresses) from unstructured input (complaint documents). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5), nor does it qualify as high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a harmonised product) or Art. 6(2) with Annex III (it performs a narrow procedural task of data extraction without influencing judicial decision-making, falling within Art. 6(3)(a)). It does not trigger transparency obligations under Art. 50 as it does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content. Therefore, it is classified as minimal_risk.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the Act (Art. 3(1)) that will be deployed by a public authority (the judiciary's publications office) to assist in the administration of justice by helping users research and interpret facts and law through plain-language queries and summaries of court decisions. This falls squarely within Annex III, point 8(a), which lists as high-risk AI systems intended to assist judicial authorities in researching and interpreting facts and law. The system does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) exception because it materially influences the outcome of legal research and interpretation, even if it does not directly advise on cases or suggest how they should be decided.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not engage prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: it does not fall under Art. 6(1) (no product safety component), and while it could fall under Annex III, point 8(b) (influencing voting behaviour), the system does not influence the outcome of elections or voting behaviour because donors are never exposed to its output and it is used only internally to prioritize outreach. Art. 6(3) applies: the system performs a preparatory task (identifying contact priorities) and does not materially influence decision-making. It triggers no transparency obligations under Art. 50 (no direct interaction with natural persons, no synthetic content generation). It is therefore minimal_risk.

The system is an AI tool for aggregating survey data and official statistics to inform the public about political sentiment through transparent analysis. Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 8(b) cover AI systems intended to influence election outcomes or voting behaviour. However, this system is explicitly designed not to influence voting decisions but to provide transparent, methodologically disclosed information to media and the public. The system does not target voters with personalized messaging, does not deploy persuasive techniques, and operates with full methodological transparency. It therefore does not pose a significant risk of materially influencing voting behaviour within the meaning of Article 6(3), and falls outside the high-risk category.

This system falls outside the scope of the EU AI Act under Article 2(6), which exempts AI systems 'specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.' The voter behavior model is developed and used exclusively for academic research, papers, and PhD theses within a university research project, with no commercial deployment, sharing with political actors, or use to influence voters.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the Act (Art. 3(1)). It is not prohibited under Art. 5. It falls under Annex III, point 8(b), as it is intended to influence the outcome of an election by automating vote counting and candidate tallying, which directly affects the election result. The exception in Art. 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making (vote counting) and does not merely perform a narrow procedural task or preparatory function. As a deployer placing the system into service in the Union, the municipality is subject to high-risk obligations under Art. 16.

The system is an AI-based editing tool that assists human writers by suggesting improvements to political communications. It does not generate synthetic content itself, only analyzes and suggests edits to human-written material. Article 50(2) requires marking of AI-generated synthetic content, but this tool performs an assistive function for standard editing without substantially altering input data or generating new content. The system does not fall under Article 5 prohibited practices, nor under Article 6 high-risk categories (Annex III, point 8(b) concerns AI systems intended to influence voting behavior or election outcomes, but this tool merely assists internal editorial review without direct exposure to voters or influence on their behavior).
